source_refs.note: Chapter 24 exercise (PDF 132-133), solved: 10 MCQs keyed (no key is printed), 11 short-answer, 3 constructed-response (reaction sequences) and 4 long questions with model answers. MCQs IV-VI and Q3(b) carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: I. Primary, secondary and tertiary amine are regarded as:
blocks.explanation: Amines of the same molecular formula, e.g. C₃H₉N: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (1°, –NH₂), CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ (2°, >NH) and (CH₃)₃N (3°, >N–), contain different amino groups, so 1°, 2° and 3° amines are regarded as functional group isomers.

blocks.prompt: II. General formula for secondary amines is:
blocks.explanation: In a secondary amine two alkyl/aryl groups are attached to an –NH– group: R–NH–R (R₂NH). RNH₂ is primary, R₃N tertiary and RCONH₂ an amide.

blocks.prompt: III. Which one of the following bases is a strongest one?
blocks.explanation: Basicity depends on the availability of the lone pair on N. Electron-donating alkyl groups (+I) increase it: diethylamine has two ethyl groups, ethylamine one (pKb 3.29), ammonia none (pKb 4.75). In phenylamine (pKb 9.38) the lone pair is delocalised into the ring. So diethylamine is the strongest base (its value is beyond the chapter's table).

blocks.prompt: IV. Acid hydrolysis if nitriles produces:
blocks.explanation: Heating a nitrile with dilute acid gives a carboxylic acid: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “if nitriles” is a misprint for “of nitriles”.

blocks.prompt: V. phenyl amine areacts with aqueous Br to form:
blocks.explanation: –NH₂ activates the ring and directs to the ortho and para positions, so all three are brominated at once: C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃NH₂ (2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, white ppt) + 3HBr.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The stem is misprinted: “areacts” should be reacts, and “aqueous Br” should be aqueous Br₂ (bromine water).

blocks.prompt: VI. Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol in NaOH to form:
blocks.explanation: This is a coupling reaction: the diazonium ion (electrophile) substitutes at the para position of phenol in mild alkaline solution, giving p-hydroxyazobenzene (an orange azo compound) with the –N=N– group: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH → C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄OH + HCl.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (a) “Phenyl hydrozine” is a misprint for phenylhydrazine (a wrong option either way).

blocks.prompt: VII. What is the structure of an azo compound:
blocks.explanation: Azo compounds contain the –N=N– (azo) group joining two groups: R₁–N=N–R₂ (e.g. Ph–N=N–Ph). R₁–NH–R₂ is a secondary amine, R–O–R an ether and R–C≡N a nitrile.

blocks.prompt: VIII. When diazonium salt is heated with water, the gas evolved is:
blocks.explanation: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → (heat) C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl. Nitrogen gas is given off and phenol forms.

blocks.prompt: IX. An aqueous solution of glycine is neutral because of the formation of:
blocks.explanation: The proton of –COOH moves to –NH₂, forming the dipolar zwitterion H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ (an internal salt) with one positive and one negative end, so there is no overall charge.

blocks.prompt: X. Which amines are produced by the reduction of amides?
blocks.explanation: Amides (–CONH₂) are reduced by LiAlH₄ in dry ether to primary amines: CH₃CONH₂ + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O. (N-substituted amides give secondary amines.)

blocks.prompt: a) Give two preparations of phenyl amine
blocks.explanation:
1. Reduction of nitrobenzene with Sn and conc. HCl: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O
2. Ammonolysis of chlorobenzene: C₆H₅Cl + 2NH₃ → (Cu₂O, 250 °C, 50 atm) C₆H₅NH₂ + NH₄Cl
(Also the Hofmann reaction of benzamide with Br₂ and NaOH.)

blocks.prompt: b) Give two preparations of secondary amines.
blocks.explanation:
1. Alkylation of a primary amine with a halogenoalkane (ethanol, pressure): CH₃CH₂Br + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + HBr
2. Reduction of an N-substituted amide: CH₃CONHCH₃ + 2H₂ → (Ni/Pt) CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + H₂O

blocks.prompt: c) What is the chromophore in azo dyes? What is its function in dyes?
blocks.explanation: The chromophore is the azo group, –N=N– (as in Ph–N=N–Ph). It is responsible for the intense colour of the dye; the colour (yellow, orange, red, blue or green) depends on the other groups attached to the benzene rings.

blocks.prompt: d) Why amides are less basic than ammonia.
blocks.explanation: In an amide the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised onto the oxygen of the C=O group (resonance), giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character. The lone pair is less available to accept H⁺, so amides are very weakly basic and give neutral solutions in water.

blocks.prompt: e) What is zwitter ion?
blocks.explanation: A zwitterion is a dipolar ion with a positive and a negative end in the same molecule, so it has no overall charge. In an α-amino acid the proton moves from –COOH to –NH₂: H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ (an internal salt); e.g. glycine, H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻.

blocks.prompt: f) Differentiate between primary, secondary & tertiary amines.
blocks.explanation: They differ in the number of alkyl/aryl groups attached to the nitrogen atom (the branching at N, not at carbon, decides the class).

rows: Soluble nitrite salt; no visible change

blocks.prompt: g) Write names & structures of four isomeric amines having the molecular formula C₃H₉N.
blocks.explanation:
1. CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂: propan-1-amine (1°)
2. CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃: propan-2-amine (1°)
3. CH₃CH₂NHCH₃: N-methylethanamine (2°)
4. (CH₃)₃N: N,N-dimethylmethanamine (3°)

blocks.prompt: h) Convert ethanamine into methanamine.
blocks.explanation:
One carbon is removed at the end by the Hofmann reaction:
CH₃CH₂NH₂ → (NaNO₂/HCl; N₂ given off) CH₃CH₂OH → (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, reflux) CH₃COOH → (SOCl₂) CH₃COCl → (NH₃) CH₃CONH₂ → (Br₂ + 4NaOH) CH₃NH₂
Last step: CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + 2NaBr + Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O (the alcohol from the unstable alkyl diazonium salt is beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: i) How will you synthesize ethanal from ethanenitrile?
blocks.explanation:
CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → (heat) CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl (acid hydrolysis)
CH₃COOH + 4[H] → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O
CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇; distil off as formed) CH₃CHO + H₂O

blocks.prompt: j) Define peptide bond. How many peptide bonds are there in a tripeptide?
blocks.explanation: A peptide bond (peptide link) is the amide bond, –CO–NH–, formed when the –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of another and a water molecule is eliminated. A tripeptide (three amino acids) has two peptide bonds.

blocks.prompt: k) Give all the tripeptides that could possibly be synthesized from glycine (Gly), alanine (Ala).
blocks.explanation:
Each of the three positions can be Gly or Ala, so 2³ = 8 tripeptides (written from the –NH₂ end):
Gly-Gly-Gly, Gly-Gly-Ala, Gly-Ala-Gly, Ala-Gly-Gly, Gly-Ala-Ala, Ala-Gly-Ala, Ala-Ala-Gly, Ala-Ala-Ala
Six of them contain both amino acids (all except Gly-Gly-Gly and Ala-Ala-Ala).

blocks.text: Complete the following reaction sequence by giving the structures of the compounds.

blocks.prompt:
a) 1, 3, 5-tribromobenzene from benzene.
benzene → (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) (A) → (Sn/HCl) (B) → (Br₂ (excess)/FeBr₃) (C) → (NaNO₂/HCl) (D) → (H₃PO₂, −N₂) (E)
blocks.explanation:
A = nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂ (nitration)
B = phenylamine, C₆H₅NH₂ (reduction: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O)
C = 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, C₆H₂Br₃NH₂: –NH₂ directs Br to both ortho and the para positions, which are meta to one another (bromine water alone is enough; FeBr₃ is not needed)
D = 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride, C₆H₂Br₃N₂⁺Cl⁻ (diazotisation below 10 °C)
E = 1,3,5-tribromobenzene, C₆H₃Br₃: H₃PO₂ replaces –N₂⁺ by H and N₂ is given off (this step is beyond the chapter). The three Br atoms are left at positions 1, 3 and 5.

blocks.prompt:
b) 1, 3, 5-Tribromobenzene from benzene.
benzene ring → (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) (A) → (Cl₂/FeCl₃) (B) → (Sn/HCl) (C) → (NaNO₂/HCl) (D) → (H₂O, −N₂) (E)
blocks.explanation:
A = nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂
B = 3-chloronitrobenzene, ClC₆H₄NO₂: –NO₂ directs the incoming Cl to the meta position (beyond the chapter)
C = 3-chlorophenylamine, ClC₆H₄NH₂ (Sn/HCl reduces –NO₂ to –NH₂)
D = 3-chlorobenzenediazonium chloride, ClC₆H₄N₂⁺Cl⁻ (diazotisation below 10 °C)
E = 3-chlorophenol, ClC₆H₄OH (warming with water: –N₂⁺ → –OH, N₂ given off)
This sequence does not give 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (see the Book correction).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part (b) repeats the heading of part (a), “1, 3, 5-Tribromobenzene from benzene”, but its reagents (Cl₂/FeCl₃ and finally H₂O) give 3-chlorophenol, not 1,3,5-tribromobenzene. The heading should name 3-chlorophenol.

blocks.prompt: c) Keep in view the scheme, devise a reaction sequence to prepare 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid from benzene.
blocks.explanation:
benzene → (CH₃Cl, anhydrous AlCl₃) methylbenzene → (conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄) 4-nitromethylbenzene (separated from the 2-isomer) → (acidified KMnO₄, heat) 4-nitrobenzoic acid → (Sn/HCl) 4-aminobenzoic acid → (NaNO₂/HCl, below 10 °C) 4-carboxybenzenediazonium chloride → (H₂O, warm, −N₂) 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, HO–C₆H₄–COOH
Order: –CH₃ is o/p-directing, so nitration is done before oxidation (–COOH would direct meta); oxidation comes before reduction so that KMnO₄ does not attack –NH₂. (The methylation and the directing effects are beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: Q4. Describe the relative basicity of aqueous ammonia, ethyl amine and phenyl amine.
blocks.explanation:
Ammonia and amines are bases because the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton. In water they partly react to give OH⁻ ions (weakly alkaline solutions):
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (pKb = 4.75)
CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ (pKb = 3.29)
C₆H₅NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ C₆H₅NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ (pKb = 9.38)
The larger the Kb (smaller the pKb), the stronger the base. Basicity depends on the availability of the lone pair on N.
Ethylamine: the ethyl group is electron donating (+I effect); it increases the electron density on N, so the lone pair is more available and ethylamine (Kb 5.1 × 10⁻⁴) is a stronger base than ammonia (Kb 1.8 × 10⁻⁵).
Phenylamine: the nitrogen is planar with its lone pair in a p orbital, which overlaps with the delocalised π electrons of the benzene ring. The lone pair is spread over the ring and is less available for a proton, so phenylamine (Kb 4.2 × 10⁻¹⁰) is a much weaker base than ammonia.
Order of basicity: ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.
Ammonia and ethylamine form salts with acids by donating the lone pair to H⁺: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄⁺Cl⁻; CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

blocks.prompt:
Q5. Give two preparation methods of each of the following.
i) Primary amines  ii) Secondary amines
blocks.explanation:
i) Primary amines:
1. From halogenoalkanes and ammonia (nucleophilic substitution): excess ethanolic ammonia under high pressure is used so that the primary amine is the main product (with excess halogenoalkane a tertiary amine forms).
CH₃CH₂Br + NH₃ (excess) → (ethanol, high pressure) CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HBr
2. Reduction of alkanenitriles with LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni):
CH₃CH₂C≡N + 4[H] → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propan-1-amine)
(Other methods: reduction of nitroalkanes, CH₃CH₂NO₂ + 3H₂ → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂NH₂ + 2H₂O; reduction of amides with LiAlH₄; and the Hofmann reaction, CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + 2NaBr + Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O, which gives an amine with one carbon less.)
ii) Secondary amines:
1. Alkylation of a primary amine: a halogenoalkane reacts with a primary amine in ethanol under pressure.
CH₃CH₂Br + CH₃NH₂ → (ethanol) CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ (N-methylethanamine) + HBr
2. Reduction of N-substituted amides:
CH₃CONHCH₃ (N-methylethanamide) + 2H₂ → (Ni/Pt) CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + H₂O

blocks.prompt: Q6. Write a note on electrophoresis.
blocks.explanation:
Electrophoresis is a technique used to separate amino acids in a mixture on the basis of their charge.
Method: a few drops of the mixture are applied to a filter paper or gel placed in a buffered solution between two electrodes, and an electric field is applied.
Principle: each amino acid has its own isoelectric point (pI), the pH at which it has no overall charge (it exists as the zwitterion).
• If pI > pH of the buffer, the amino acid is mainly positively charged and moves towards the cathode (negative electrode).
• If pI < pH, it is mainly negatively charged and moves towards the anode (positive electrode).
• If pI = pH, it has no net charge and does not move.
The greater the difference between pI and pH, the faster it moves. If two amino acids have very similar pI values (e.g. glycine and leucine), the one with the larger molecular mass moves more slowly, because the charge has to carry a greater mass.
Example (pH 6): lysine (pI 9.74) moves towards the cathode, alanine (pI 6.02) stays almost at the start, and glutamic acid (pI 3.22) moves towards the anode.
Detection: amino acids are colourless, so the paper is sprayed with ninhydrin (locating agent), which reacts with amino acids to give a purple product, showing the spots.
Use: electrophoresis is an analytical method for finding the number of amino acids in a mixture; it cannot separate large quantities, for which other techniques such as column chromatography are used.

blocks.prompt: Q7. Explain the formation of azo compounds from phenylamine and illustrate the preparation of a dye using this?
blocks.explanation:
Step 1: Diazotisation. Nitrous acid is unstable, so it is made in situ from sodium nitrite and HCl, and the mixture is kept below 10 °C with ice:
NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl
C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → (below 10 °C) C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ (benzenediazonium chloride) + 2H₂O
The low temperature is needed because diazonium salts decompose, giving off N₂, even at room temperature. Aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperature because the positive charge is delocalised over the ring (alkyl diazonium salts cannot be isolated).
Step 2: Coupling. The diazonium ion is an electrophile; it reacts with a strongly activated aromatic compound (a phenol in mild alkaline solution, or an aromatic amine in mild acidic solution) and substitutes at the para position. The product contains the –N=N– (azo) group and is called an azo compound.
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH → (NaOH) C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH (p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange solid) + HCl
Mechanism (in words): the lone pair of the –OH oxygen pushes electrons into the ring; the ring π electrons at the para carbon attack the terminal N of Ph–N≡N⁺; the intermediate then loses H⁺ from that carbon and the ring becomes aromatic again, giving the azo compound.
Preparation of a dye:
Butter yellow: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂ (N,N-dimethylphenylamine) → (CH₃COOH) (CH₃)₂N–C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₅ (p-dimethylaminoazobenzene) + HCl. It was once used in food but is now forbidden because it is carcinogenic.
Similarly, diazotised sulfanilic acid coupled with N,N-dimethylphenylamine gives methyl orange, an acid–base indicator.
The azo group (Ph–N=N–Ph) is the chromophore: it gives the dyes their intense colours, from yellow and orange to red, blue and green, depending on the other groups on the rings.
